theory.intro: For a positive deposit and fixed positive rates, with no extra deposits or withdrawals, simple interest uses the **original deposit** each year. Compound interest uses the **current balance**, including earlier interest. Here compounding is annual.
facts: Simple interest is $I = Prn$, so the balance after $n$ years is $P + Prn$.
Compound interest is $FV = PV(1+r)^{n}$, so the interest earned is $FV - PV$.
With the same positive deposit and positive annual rate, simple and annually compounded balances are equal after one year; compound interest is greater after further whole years.
For positive rates, a higher simple rate can give more over a short term than a lower compound rate. Compare the totals for the stated term.
With a positive deposit and positive annual rates, the simple-interest balance is a straight line; the compound-interest balance curves upwards and gets steeper.
Work out each total in one calculation and round only at the end, or the difference shifts by cents.
steps: Find the total from the simple interest offer.
Find the total from the compound interest offer.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) $\$1200$ earns $5\%$ p.a. for $3$ years. Compare simple interest with annual compounding: how much extra interest does compounding earn?
(b) What is the difference if the same investment is held for only one year?
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Simple interest $=1200\times0.05\times3=\$180$.
Compound balance $=1200(1.05)^3=\$1389.15$.
Compound interest $=1389.15-1200=\$189.15$.
Extra interest $=189.15-180=\$9.15$.
(b) Both earn $1200\times0.05=\$60$ in the first year, so the difference is $\$0$.

workedExamples.question_text: A deposit of $\$3600$ can earn $8\%$ p.a. simple interest with $A$, or $7\%$ p.a. compounded annually with $B$. Compare their final balances (a) after $3$ years and (b) after $6$ years. Give each winning margin to the nearest cent.

Both accounts start with $\$3200$ and earn $5\%$ p.a.; one is simple and one compounds annually. Which account is compound, and why?
$\begin{array}{c|rrr}\text{Year}&1&2&3\\\hline M&3360&3520&3680\\N&3360&3528&3704.40\end{array}$
workedExamples.solution_text:
$M$ increases by $\$160$ each year.
$N$ increases by $\$160$, $\$168$ and $\$176.40$.
$N$ is the compound account: its interest uses each new balance. $M$ uses the original deposit each year.

(a) $A$ is the straight line, with the same dollar rise each year, so it is simple interest. $B$ curves upwards as its yearly interest grows, so it is compound interest.
(b) At $3$ years, line $A$ gives $\$2600$. This is $2000+2000(0.10)(3)$.

workedExamples.question_text:
$\$4200$ earns $6\%$ p.a., once as simple interest and once compounded annually. Find the extra compound interest (a) after $3$ years and (b) after $6$ years, to the nearest cent.
(c) How many times as large is the second difference, to one decimal place?
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Gap $=4200(1.06)^3-[4200+4200(0.06)(3)]$
$=\$46.2672\approx\$46.27$.
(b) Gap $=4200(1.06)^6-[4200+4200(0.06)(6)]$
$\approx\$245.78$.
(c) Divide the unrounded second gap by the unrounded first gap:
$\dfrac{4200(1.06)^6-5712}{46.2672}\approx5.3$.
It is $5.3$ times as large; doubling the time does not double the gap.

workedExamples.question_text: The same deposit earns $10\%$ p.a. for $2$ years, once with simple interest and once compounded annually. The compound account earns $\$47$ more. Find the deposit.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Let the deposit be $P$.
Compound balance $=P(1.10)^2=1.21P$.
Simple balance $=P+P(0.10)(2)=1.20P$.
Their difference is $0.01P=47$.
$P=47\div0.01=\$4700$.

workedExamples.question_text: A deposit of $\$4600$ earns $7.5\%$ p.a. simple interest with $A$, or $6.4\%$ p.a. compounded annually with $B$. Find the first whole year when $B$ is ahead and its margin at that time, to the nearest cent.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Try whole years using $A=4600+345n$ and $B=4600(1.064)^n$.
At $n=5$: $A=\$6325$ and $B\approx\$6272.87$, so $A$ is ahead.
At $n=6$: $A=\$6670$ and $B\approx\$6674.33$, so $B$ is ahead.
The first whole year is $6$.
Margin $=4600(1.064)^6-6670\approx\$4.33$.

workedExamples.question_text: $\$4800$ earns $6.5\%$ p.a. compounded annually for $4$ years. Find the simple annual rate that earns the same total interest over those years, to two decimal places.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Compound interest $I=4800(1.065)^4-4800$.
For the same interest, $I=4800\times r\times4$.
$r=\dfrac{4800(1.065)^4-4800}{4800\times4}$.
As a percentage, $r\approx7.16\%$ p.a. Keep the unrounded compound interest when dividing.

workedExamples.question_text: $\$6000$ earns $6\%$ p.a., once as simple interest and once compounded annually. In which year does the compound account first earn over $\$60$ more interest in that single year?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Simple interest is $6000(0.06)=\$360$ each year, so the compound account must earn over $\$420$ in one year.
Year $3$ interest $=6000(1.06)^2(0.06)=\$404.496$.
Year $4$ interest $=6000(1.06)^3(0.06)=\$428.76576$.
The yearly compound interest increases, so year $4$ is the first year above $\$420$.

foundation.question_text:
$\$8000$ is invested for $4$ years at $5\%$ p.a.
How much more interest does an account paying compound interest earn than an account paying simple interest, to the nearest cent?

A credit union offers $6\%$ p.a. simple interest and a bank offers $6\%$ p.a. compounding annually.
$\$15\,000$ is invested with each for $3$ years.
Find the difference between the two final balances, to the nearest cent.

$\$6000$ is invested for $1$ year, one account at $7\%$ p.a. simple interest and one at $7\%$ p.a. compounding annually.
How much more interest does the compound account earn?
foundation.solution_text:
$I = 6000\times0.07\times1$
$=\$420$
$FV = 6000(1.07)^{1}$
$=\$6420$, so the compound interest is also $\$420$.
Difference $=420-420$
$=\$0$

foundation.question_text:
$\$4000$ is invested for $2$ years at $10\%$ p.a.
How much more interest does an account paying compound interest earn than an account paying simple interest?

A bank offers $4.5\%$ p.a. simple interest and a credit union offers $4.5\%$ p.a. compounding annually.
$\$12\,000$ is invested with each for $5$ years.
How much more interest does the credit union account earn, to the nearest cent?

The table shows the balance of two accounts, each opened with $\$9000$ at $5\%$ p.a.
One pays simple interest and the other compounds annually.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}\text{Year}&1&2&3\\\hline \text{Account M}&\$9450&\$9900&\$10\,350\\\hline \text{Account N}&\$9450&\$9922.50&\$10\,418.63\end{array}$
Which account pays compound interest?
Give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
Account M rises by $\$450$ every year, a constant amount.
Account N rises by $\$450$, then $\$472.50$, then $\$496.13$, a growing amount.
Account N pays compound interest, because each year's interest is calculated on the new balance and so is larger than the year before.

development.question_text:
Bank A offers $7\%$ p.a. simple interest.
Credit union B offers $6\%$ p.a. compounding annually.
$\$9000$ is invested for $5$ years.
Which gives the greater final balance, and by how much, to the nearest cent?

Bank A offers $7\%$ p.a. simple interest and credit union B offers $6\%$ p.a. compounding annually.
$\$9000$ is invested for $10$ years.
Which gives the greater final balance, and by how much, to the nearest cent?
development.solution_text:
Bank A: $9000+9000\times0.07\times10$
$=\$15\,300$
Credit union B: $9000(1.06)^{10}$
$=\$16\,117.63$
Difference $=16\,117.63-15\,300$
$=\$817.63$
Credit union B gives the greater balance, by $\$817.63$.

development.question_text:
$\$6000$ is invested at $8\%$ p.a., once as simple interest and once compounding annually.
Find the difference between the two balances after $3$ years and after $6$ years, each to the nearest cent, and state how many times as large the second difference is, to $1$ decimal place.

The same amount is invested for $4$ years in two accounts, one at $9\%$ p.a. simple interest and one at $9\%$ p.a. compounding annually.
The compound account earns $\$386.86$ more interest.
Find the amount invested, to the nearest dollar.

The table shows the balance of two accounts, each opened with $\$20\,000$ at $7\%$ p.a.
One pays simple interest and the other compounds annually.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}\text{Year}&1&2&3&4\\\hline \text{Simple}&\$21\,400&\$22\,800&\$24\,200&\$25\,600\\\hline \text{Compound}&\$21\,400&\$22\,898.00&\$24\,500.86&\$26\,215.92\end{array}$
Find the difference between the two balances after year $4$, and state what is happening to the difference from year to year.
development.solution_text:
Difference after year $4$ $=26\,215.92-25\,600$
$=\$615.92$
The differences are $\$0$, $\$98$, $\$300.86$ and $\$615.92$, so the gap widens every year, because the compound account earns interest on interest already paid.

development.question_text:
Offer A pays $10\%$ p.a. simple interest and Offer B pays $8\%$ p.a. compounding annually, on a deposit of $\$4000$.
Find the first whole year in which Offer B is ahead of Offer A.
development.solution_text:
Offer A: $4000+400n$
Offer B: $4000(1.08)^{n}$
$n=6$: $\$6400$ and $\$6347.50$, so A is ahead.
$n=7$: $\$6800$ and $\$6855.30$, so B is ahead.
Offer B is first ahead after $7$ years.

mastery.question_text:
$\$25\,000$ is invested at $6.4\%$ p.a. compounding annually for $6$ years.
Find the simple interest rate that would earn the same total interest over those $6$ years, correct to $2$ decimal places.
mastery.solution_text:
Compound interest $I=25000(1.064)^6-25000$.
For the same interest, $I=25000\times r\times6$.
$r=\dfrac{25000(1.064)^6-25000}{25000\times6}$.
Keep the full calculator value; as a percentage, $r\approx7.52\%$ p.a.

mastery.question_text:
Offer A pays $9\%$ p.a. simple interest and Offer B pays $7\%$ p.a. compounding annually, on a deposit of $\$12\,000$.
Find the first whole year in which Offer B is ahead of Offer A, and how far ahead it is at that time, to the nearest cent.

$\$10\,000$ is invested at $5\%$ p.a., once as simple interest and once compounding annually.
In which year does the compound account first earn more than $\$100$ more interest in that single year than the simple account earns?
mastery.solution_text:
The simple account earns $10\,000\times0.05=\$500$ each year, so the compound account must earn more than $\$600$ in one year.
Interest in year $n$ $=10\,000(1.05)^{n-1}\times0.05$
$n=4$: $10\,000(1.05)^{3}\times0.05=\$578.81$
$n=5$: $10\,000(1.05)^{4}\times0.05=\$607.75$
The compound account first earns more than $\$100$ extra in a single year in year $5$.
